title: Hash maps and the other collections
summary: HashMap<K, V> for lookups by key: inserting, reading, ownership of keys and values, overwriting, the entry API, counting words; and when to choose BTreeMap, HashSet, BTreeSet or VecDeque instead.

sections: TRPL 8.3 Storing Keys with Associated Values in Hash Maps
TRPL 8.3 Accessing Values in a Hash Map
TRPL 8.3 Managing Ownership in Hash Maps
PR ch16 HashMap<K, V> and BTreeMap<K, V>

blocks.md: A **hash map**, `HashMap<K, V>`, stores values of type `V` looked up by keys of type `K`. Other languages call it a dictionary, an associative array or an object. Use it whenever you want to find something by a key rather than by position: a score by team name, a price by product id, a count by word.

blocks.explain: `HashMap` is not in the prelude, so it needs a `use`. `get` returns `Option<&V>`: `copied()` turns `Option<&i32>` into `Option<i32>`, and `unwrap_or(0)` supplies a default. A `HashMap<String, _>` can be searched with a `&str`, which is why `get("Red")` works.

blocks.title: Iterating
blocks.md: `for (key, value) in &scores` visits every pair. The order is **arbitrary** and may change between runs: a hash map arranges entries by the hash of the key, not by insertion or sort order. If you need sorted keys, use `BTreeMap` (below).

blocks.explain: `BTreeMap` has the same methods but keeps keys sorted, so iteration is in key order. This example uses it so the output is predictable.

blocks.title: Ownership
blocks.md: For `Copy` types like `i32`, values are copied into the map. Owned values like `String` are **moved** in, and the map becomes their owner:

blocks.output:
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `field_name`
 --> src/main.rs:8:16
  |
4 |     let field_name = String::from("Favorite color");
  |         ---------- move occurs because `field_name` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
...
7 |     map.insert(field_name, field_value);
  |                ---------- value moved here
8 |     println!("{field_name}");
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
7 |     map.insert(field_name.clone(), field_value);
  |                          ++++++++
blocks.explain: Insert references instead (`&str`) and the map does not own them, but then the borrowed data must outlive the map. Chapter 10's lifetimes are what the compiler uses to check that.

blocks.title: Updating
blocks.md:
Each key has at most one value. When a key already exists you have three choices:

1. **Overwrite**: `insert` again replaces the old value (and returns it as `Some(old)`).
2. **Insert only if absent**: `entry(key).or_insert(value)`.
3. **Update based on the old value**: `or_insert` returns a `&mut V` to the value, new or existing, so you can change it.

The **entry API** in options 2 and 3 looks up the key once, then lets you act on the slot whether or not it was filled.

blocks.explain: `count` is a `&mut i32` pointing into the map; `*count += 1` changes the stored value. The mutable borrow ends at the end of each loop pass.

blocks.title: Hashing
blocks.md: By default `HashMap` uses SipHash, which resists denial-of-service attacks where someone sends keys chosen to collide. It is not the fastest hash. If profiling shows hashing matters and the keys are trusted, crates such as `ahash` or `fxhash` provide faster hashers. Keys must implement `Eq` and `Hash`; `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` makes your own types usable as keys.

rows: a list with fast add/remove at both ends
fast lookup by key, order does not matter
you need sorted output or ranges of keys
priority queues: always take the biggest

blocks.explain: `collect()` can build any collection from an iterator; the type annotation says which. `HashSet::insert` returns `false` when the value was already there, which makes "first repeat" a one-liner.

blocks.title: Group by first letter
blocks.md: Group the names by their first letter into a `BTreeMap<char, Vec<&str>>` and print it. Use the entry API: `entry(letter).or_insert_with(Vec::new).push(name)` (or `or_default()`).
hints: `for name in names`, then `let letter = name.chars().next().unwrap();`.
`groups.entry(letter).or_default().push(name);` creates an empty Vec the first time a letter is seen.

blocks.title: Company directory
blocks.goal: Use maps and sets to answer questions about data, as in The Rust Programming Language's end-of-chapter exercise.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn word_frequencies(text: &str) -> HashMap<String, usize>`: lowercase every word (split on whitespace) and count it.
- `pub fn add_employee(dir: &mut BTreeMap<String, Vec<String>>, command: &str) -> bool`: commands look like `"Add Sally to Engineering"`. Add the name to that department and return `true`; anything else returns `false` and changes nothing.
- `pub fn department_list(dir: &BTreeMap<String, Vec<String>>, dept: &str) -> Vec<String>`: the names in that department sorted alphabetically (empty if none).
- `pub fn unique_letters(word: &str) -> usize`: how many different chars the word has.
hints: `add_employee`: `let words: Vec<&str> = command.split_whitespace().collect();` then match the slice: `if let ["Add", name, "to", dept] = words.as_slice() { ... }`.
`unique_letters`: collect the chars into a `HashSet<char>` and take its `len()`.
blocks.solution_explain: The slice pattern `["Add", name, "to", dept]` checks the shape of the whole command and binds the two parts in one step; chapter 19 covers slice patterns. `cloned()` turns `Option<&Vec<String>>` into `Option<Vec<String>>` so the result can be sorted without touching the directory.

Which collection answers "is this id already used?" quickly, with no values attached?

questions.q: Iterating over a `HashMap` always returns entries in insertion order.
questions.explanation: The order is arbitrary; use `BTreeMap` for sorted order.

points: `HashMap<K, V>` maps keys to values; `use std::collections::HashMap;`.
`get` returns `Option<&V>`; owned keys and values are moved into the map.
`insert` overwrites; `entry(k).or_insert(v)` inserts only if absent and returns `&mut V` for updating.
Hash map order is arbitrary; `BTreeMap` keeps keys sorted.
Sets (`HashSet`, `BTreeSet`) hold unique values; `VecDeque` is a double-ended queue; `BinaryHeap` a priority queue.

terms.def: A collection that maps keys to values using hashing; lookups are fast and order is arbitrary.
map.entry(key) gives access to a key's slot whether or not it exists, for insert-or-update in one lookup.
A map that keeps its keys sorted.
A collection of unique values with fast membership tests.
A growable ring buffer with fast push and pop at both ends.
